chunks: Buck failure modes, detection and prevention. The question: What are some failure modes of buck converters? How can they be detected and prevented?
A buck converter can fail in a handful of predictable ways, and you can sort them by part. The switches can overheat, overlap, or see too much voltage. The inductor can saturate.
The input voltage can bounce up (ring) or dip (sag), the output can overshoot, and the capacitors can wear out.
Good designs add protections and margins to prevent each one, and ways to detect it.
Think of inspecting a house room by room. In the plumbing you look for leaks, in the wiring for overload, and in the roof for storm damage.
Each room has its own typical problem and its own safeguard. A buck is the same: each block has its usual failure and its usual guard.
The house picture does not show one buck-specific danger: both switches on at once, which is a short from the input to ground.
With a fixed frequency the inductor gains about 0. 18 amps every 2 microseconds cycle and reaches 6 amps in roughly 33 microseconds.
Quartering the frequency lengthens the off-time so each cycle discharges more current, cutting the net rise rate by about a factor of eight (to about 0.
012 amps/µs); hiccup then cuts power before it matters. The model uses a constant 0. 1 volts output and fixed minimum on-time; real behaviour has resistive drops that also help.
Shoot-through: both switches on at the same time, shorting the input to ground. Dead time: a short gap when both switches are off, to prevent shoot-through.
Saturation: the inductor's core is full, so its current runs away ("Inductor saturation current and DCR vs ACR").
Current limit: a protection that turns the switch off when the current gets too high. UVLO / OVP: under-voltage lockout and over-voltage protection.
Say a 12 volts input drives two switches, each with 10 milliohms of resistance. If both turn on together, the input sees about 20 milliohms. In principle that is 12 over 0.
02 equals 600 amps, limited in practice by the capacitor and the wiring, but it can still destroy the part in moments.
The fix is dead time: turn one off, wait a few nanoseconds, then turn the other on. That is the whole idea.

"By block: in the switches, shoot-through and switch-node overshoot, prevented with dead time and a tight hot loop; in the inductor, saturation, prevented by choosing I sat above the current limit; on shorts, current runaway handled by current limit with foldback and hiccup; on the input, hot-plug ringing to twice V IN and brown-outs, handled by damping, TVS and UVLO; on the output, overshoot and overvoltage handled by soft-start and OVP.
Then loop instability and wear-out. Detection is power-good and fault flags plus scope checks of the switch node, current and output."
